At a Glance
Before reentering after an earthquake, wait for official clearance when available, inspect the building from outside, and check for structural damage, fire, gas, electrical, water, and falling-object hazards. Stay out if you see leaning walls, shifted foundations, major cracks, separated framing, damaged chimneys, downed wires, broken gas lines, or unusual sounds. Even a building that looks intact may have weakened connections or hidden utility damage, and aftershocks can turn minor damage into a collapse risk. If you must retrieve essential items, use a brief, planned entry only when the structure appears stable, utilities are safe, exits remain clear, and another adult knows where you are. Leave immediately if conditions change.
What you’ll learn
This guide covers the following practical points:
Wait for Clearance and Assess the Exterior
— Reentering begins with information, not a doorway inspection.
Recognize Structural Damage That Makes Entry Unsafe — Structural damage affects the building’s ability to carry weight and resist another movement.
Check Gas, Electrical, Water, and Fire Hazards — Utility damage is a separate entry decision from structural damage.
Make a Short, Controlled Entry When Conditions Permit — A permitted entry should be brief, purposeful, and reversible.
Wait for Clearance and Assess the Exterior
Reentering begins with information, not a doorway inspection. Local emergency managers, fire officials, building officials, or utility providers may issue instructions about evacuation zones, damaged structures, gas shutoffs, and restricted streets. Follow those directions before making a personal assessment. An official warning may account for hazards that are not visible from your property, such as a nearby chemical release, unstable neighboring building, blocked access route, or damaged bridge.
From a safe location outside, look at the building as a whole. Compare its present shape with what you know from before the earthquake. A roofline that sags, a wall that appears to lean, a porch that has pulled away, or a chimney that has shifted deserves more caution than an isolated cosmetic crack in plaster. Check whether doors and windows are jammed, whether the foundation has moved, and whether exterior stairs, decks, balconies, and overhead attachments remain connected.
Do not walk directly beneath masonry, balconies, glass, roof edges, or damaged power lines while inspecting. Keep children and pets away from the structure. If you smell gas, see smoke, hear hissing, observe sparks, or notice a broken water main, move away and contact the appropriate emergency or utility service from a safe location. A common mistake is treating the absence of flames as proof that entry is safe; gas accumulation, unstable masonry, and concealed electrical damage can exist without an active fire.
Take photographs from a distance if doing so does not delay evacuation or expose you to danger. They can help a building professional, insurer, or emergency official understand changes, but photographs do not replace an inspection. A building may look nearly normal from the street while a crawlspace, chimney, connection, or interior partition has failed.
Recognize Structural Damage That Makes Entry Unsafe
Structural damage affects the building’s ability to carry weight and resist another movement. Earthquakes can shift foundations, deform frames, loosen roof connections, separate walls from floors, and damage chimneys or parapets. The most serious
warning signs
are changes in alignment, separation, displacement, and loss of support rather than surface cracking alone.
Stay out and request professional evaluation if you see a leaning wall, a collapsed or partially collapsed floor, a visibly shifted foundation, large cracks in structural walls, separated framing, buckled columns, heavy debris pressing against a wall, or a stairway that has pulled away from the building. A damaged chimney is especially dangerous because bricks or sections can fall during an aftershock even when the main walls appear sound. Do not enter beneath a damaged roof or beside a wall that has bulged outward.
Interior clues can confirm a problem but should not be sought by taking unnecessary risks. Doors that suddenly bind, floors that feel sloped, unusual gaps around frames, cracked beams, broken supports, and fresh daylight where none existed before indicate movement. A few hairline cracks in nonstructural drywall may be less concerning than one displaced support, but a nonexpert should not rely on visual grading to clear a building.

Consider the difference between a quick retrieval and normal occupancy. Entering briefly to obtain medication may be justified only if authorities have not prohibited entry, the exterior appears stable, utilities are controlled, and a competent professional or official has not identified a danger. Returning to sleep, cook, shower, or clean up requires a much higher level of confidence because longer exposure increases the chance of encountering aftershocks, fire, leaks, or falling contents.
Never move heavy debris or prop a damaged wall yourself. Shifting one object can remove temporary support and cause a secondary collapse. If someone may be trapped, call emergency services and provide the exact location rather than entering a damaged structure for a rescue attempt.
Check Gas, Electrical, Water, and Fire Hazards
Utility damage is a separate entry decision from
structural damage
. Earthquake movement can break gas piping, pull electrical conductors from fittings, rupture water lines, and damage appliances. These failures may create delayed hazards: a small leak can spread through a closed room, a live wire can energize wet surfaces, and water can weaken ceilings or contact electrical equipment.
Do not use matches, lighters, candles, cigarettes, light switches, appliances, or vehicle engines near a suspected gas leak. If you smell gas or hear a hissing sound, leave immediately and call the gas utility or emergency services from outside. Do not assume that opening a window or turning off a valve makes the building safe enough to search. Only operate a gas shutoff if you know the valve, can reach it without entering an unsafe area, and local guidance supports that action; utilities may need to restore service and inspect the system before relighting appliances.
Look for fallen wires, damaged service equipment, sparks, smoke, scorched outlets, and water near electrical panels or appliances. Treat every downed wire as energized, including one that appears inactive. Do not enter standing water where electrical equipment may be present. If the main electrical panel is damaged, wet, sparking, or inaccessible, leave it to qualified personnel.
Water problems require judgment rather than an automatic shutoff. A burst pipe may be wasting water and damaging the structure, while shutting off supply can remove water needed for firefighting or sanitation. If a safe, accessible main valve is known and officials recommend shutting it, do so; otherwise report the leak. Do not drink tap water until the water provider or local health authority says it is safe, particularly when pipes, wells, or pressure systems have been damaged.
Check for small fires, hot smoke, damaged heating equipment, fallen lamps, and combustible materials near ignition sources. Keep a clear route to the exit and carry a flashlight rather than using an open flame. A phone light may help for a very short look, but it can fail, leave both hands occupied, and provide poor warning of trip hazards. The practical priority is to identify hazards from outside and call trained responders, not to make the property fully functional before it has been cleared.
Make a Short, Controlled Entry When Conditions Permit
A permitted entry should be brief, purposeful, and reversible. Decide the single most important task before opening the door, such as retrieving essential medication, identification, a communication device, or a pet carrier. Avoid entering to sort belongings, inspect every room, or begin cleanup. Those tasks increase time inside and may disturb debris that is supporting other material.
Use sturdy footwear, gloves, eye protection, and a hard hat if one is available. Wear long sleeves and keep a flashlight accessible. Do not enter alone; have another adult remain outside, maintain communication, and know the planned exit. If the person outside cannot reach you or notices a new hazard, the entry should end immediately. Do not use elevators, stand beneath damaged ceilings, or walk across unstable floors.
Move slowly and stay near the route you already assessed. Do not touch unknown liquids, exposed wiring, damaged appliances, or fallen containers. Watch for broken glass, nails, shifted furniture, leaking pipes, and objects that may fall during an aftershock. Keep doors open only if doing so does not create another hazard, and never block the exit with bags or debris.
A simple retrieval sequence reduces impulsive decisions:
Confirm that officials have not ordered people to stay out.
Recheck the exterior, entryway, utilities, and exit path.
Tell another person the exact task and expected time.
Take only the predetermined items.
Leave at once if you hear cracking, feel movement, smell gas, see smoke, or lose the exit route.
The common failure is allowing a short entry to become a normal visit. Once inside, people often notice additional belongings and stay longer than planned. A written retrieval list and a strict time limit counter that pressure. If a needed item is buried, blocked, or located near damage, abandon it and ask responders or a building professional for help rather than improvising.
Leave Again Aftershocks or New Damage Appear
Aftershocks can produce new failures in a building that survived the main earthquake. They may dislodge masonry, shift furniture, rupture a repaired-looking pipe, or worsen a crack that was not obviously dangerous earlier. Reentry is therefore not a one-time clearance; conditions must be reassessed whenever the building moves, weather changes, utilities behave differently, or new sounds and odors appear.
Leave immediately if an aftershock causes visible movement, falling debris, new cracking, doors to jam, a utility odor, smoke, sparks, water intrusion, or a change in the building’s shape. Do not remain inside to finish a task or collect more items. Move away from the structure and wait for updated instructions. If you are sheltering nearby, choose an open area away from walls, chimneys, glass, utility lines, and damaged trees.
Before normal reoccupancy, arrange evaluation by the authority or qualified professional appropriate to the damage. A visual walk-through by a neighbor or landlord may identify obvious problems but cannot establish that hidden framing, foundations, gas piping, or electrical systems are safe. Ask specifically what was inspected, what remains restricted, and whether utilities require separate approval.
Record damage without disturbing it, preserve receipts for emergency work, and follow instructions from insurers and public agencies. Do not make permanent repairs before documenting conditions unless immediate action is necessary to prevent further harm. Keep household members out until the building has been cleared for the type of use you intend; permission to retrieve an item is not automatically permission to live there.
Use What to do after an earthquake before reentering as a decision reminder, not a substitute for local orders or a professional inspection. The safest choice may be inconvenience, lost belongings, or a delayed return. Those costs are preferable to adding an avoidable exposure to a weakened structure.
Frequently Asked Questions
How long should I wait before going back inside after an earthquake?
Wait for official clearance when available. If no official inspection is available, do not enter until the exterior, utilities, structure, and exit route appear safe, and leave immediately if conditions change.
Can I enter briefly to get medicine or identification?
Only if authorities have not prohibited entry and the building shows no serious damage or utility hazard. Use a short retrieval plan, protective footwear, an outside monitor, and abandon the task if anything seems unstable.
What does a gas leak smell like after an earthquake?
Natural gas is commonly given a sulfur-like odor, but smell is not a reliable safety test. Leave immediately for any suspected leak, avoid switches and flames, and call the utility or emergency services from outside.
Are cracks in the walls always a reason to stay out?
Not every surface crack indicates structural failure, but fresh, widening, diagonal, or extensive cracks require caution. Cracks accompanied by leaning, separation, shifted floors, jammed doors, or damaged supports warrant professional evaluation before entry.
Is a building safe to occupy if it looks normal from outside?
No. Hidden damage to framing, foundations, chimneys, wiring, gas piping, or water systems may not be visible from the street. Exterior appearance is a screening step, not proof that normal occupancy is safe.
Conclusion
Reentry after an earthquake should be treated as a controlled risk decision, not a routine return home. Follow official instructions first, inspect from a distance, and treat leaning structures, displaced foundations, damaged chimneys, exposed wiring, gas odors, smoke, standing water, and blocked exits as reasons to stay out. A brief retrieval may be possible in an apparently stable building, but it should involve one defined task, protective clothing, an outside contact, and a clear exit. Normal living requires more than a quick look; utilities and concealed structural elements may need professional clearance. Reassess after every aftershock and leave immediately when new damage, movement, sounds, odors, or leaks appear.
